body.heading: A keyboard split in two
paragraphs: Touch-typing divides the QWERTY keyboard down the middle: your left hand owns Q, W, E, R, T and the rows beneath them; your right hand owns the rest. Most words need both hands, passing letters back and forth like a relay.

But some words live entirely on one side. 'Stewardesses' — twelve letters — uses only left-hand letters: S, T, E, W, A, R, D. It is often called the longest common English word typeable with one hand, and you can verify it right now by hovering your left hand over the keys and spelling it out.

body.heading: Records and near-records
paragraphs: The right hand's champion is shorter and sweeter: 'lollipop', all right-hand letters. Other left-hand residents include 'watercress', 'desegregated' and 'aftereffects' — words that feel two-handed until you check.

A different keyboard curiosity lives in 'bookkeeping': it contains three double letters in a row — oo, kk, ee — a little staircase hiding in an ordinary word. Its longer cousin 'subbookkeeper' manages four in a row.

body.heading: Test your name
paragraphs: Now check the words that matter to you: your name, your street, your favourite food. Which hand does each one favour? Most words lean heavily to one side without ever going all the way.

It is a five-minute investigation with a strange payoff — you will never quite unsee the geography of the keyboard, and every long word you type becomes a tiny question: could one hand have done this alone?

takeaway: Every letter of 'stewardesses' lives under your left hand — the keyboard is quietly full of these little patterns.
